I chose candidate 6, after a rough mental pass on forecast values. I didn't simulate any plan day by day.

**Common to all plans.** The opening stock (57 / 32) covers only part of the demand for days 0–2. Nothing arrives before day 3, so every plan takes about the same shortage at the start.

**Daily ordering (3, 7).** These pay the 58 fee about 27 times instead of 14, roughly 750 extra in fees. Plan 3 also orders about at the forecast, while average demand is about 4.6% above it. So it slowly runs short, and each missing unit costs 8 plus the lost margin. Plan 7 orders about 10% above forecast, so it avoids that, but the fee gap alone outweighs this.

**Ordering every 2 days, small quantities (0, 2).** Plan 0 orders exactly the forecast and plan 2 about 4% above it. Since orders are fixed, any shortfall carries over from period to period and isn't corrected. Average demand is higher than these orders, so stock drifts toward zero and shortages become frequent. A missing unit costs about 11 for product 0 and 14 for product 1. An extra unit mostly carries to the next period for 0.4–0.7 a day in storage, so holding extra is cheap.

**Ordering every 2 days, about 20% over (1).** The surplus builds by about 13 units of product 0 per 2-day period. That runs into the 236 capacity limit, so excess deliveries are lost on arrival, and the old stock spoils. It wastes several hundred on purchases that never sell.

**Ordering every 3 days (4).** This saves about 290 in fees. But each delivery is around 210 units on top of existing stock, so it often goes over 236 and the excess is lost. It also runs short before the next delivery arrives.

**Ordering every 2 days, about 10% over (5, 6).** The buffer grows only modestly, which is about the right cover for random demand. The two plans differ only at the end:
- **Plan 5** skips the day-26 order, saving 58. But its 180 units arrive on day 27 on top of roughly 100 units of accumulated stock. That likely exceeds 236, so part of the product 1 delivery is lost, followed by shortages in the last days.
- **Plan 6** splits the same amount into 133 + 51 units. That stays close to the capacity limit, so it is the safer plan.

Plan 6 should have the highest expected profit and is also more robust if actual demand differs from the forecast.

I'd pick **candidate 5** as the best expected result.

**Order cycle.** Every plan except 3, 4 and 7 orders every 2 days with a 3-day delivery time. So each delivery has to cover 2 days of sales. The first delivery arrives on day 3. Days 0–2 sell out for every plan, because the starting stock (57 and 32) can't cover that demand.

**Why ordering above forecast pays.**
- Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, not the forecast itself.
- Running short costs a lot: about 11 per unit for product 0 (lost margin 3 + penalty 8) and about 14 for product 1 (margin 6 + penalty 8).
- Having extra costs little. Shelf life is 9 and 7 days, so leftovers roll into the next cycle and cost only 0.7 or 0.4 a day to store.
- So plans ordering at forecast level, close to expected demand, lose more to penalties: candidates 0, 2 and 3.

**Why not too far above forecast.** The plan is fixed and doesn't react to actual sales. Candidate 1 orders about 1.2 × forecast, which beats average demand by about 15% a cycle. That surplus builds up by roughly 20 units of both products together each cycle. With 236 places, it soon hits the warehouse limit, and overflow is lost after being paid for. Old batches also start to expire. Candidates 6 and 5 order about 1.1 × forecast. That builds a modest safety stock without overflowing.

**Candidates 4 and 7.**
- Candidate 4 orders every 3 days. That saves on the 58 fee but brings in big deliveries of 216 units or more, so it risks overflow. It's also short for the day-9 spike in product 0 (153 against about 183 needed for days 9–11).
- Candidate 7 orders every day, paying the 58 fee 27 times, which costs about 750 more than the every-other-day plans.

**Candidate 5 vs 6.** They are identical up to day 22. On day 24, candidate 5 orders 112 and 68 to cover days 27–29 (demand about 107 and 62) and skips the day-26 order. That saves one 58 fee, and the bigger stock costs little in storage. So 5 comes out slightly ahead of 6.

I picked **candidate 5**, with moderate confidence. Candidates 5 and 6 are almost tied, and 5 wins only in the last days. I worked this out by reasoning, not by running a simulation.

1. **Order frequency.** Each ordering day costs a 58 fee. Ordering every day (candidates 3 and 7) adds about 13 extra fees, roughly 750. With the 2-day cycle, storage costs about 19 per day more than ordering daily, about 38 per cycle. That is less than the 58 fee it saves. The 3-day cycle (candidate 4) saves one fee every 6 days but adds about 115 in storage over the same 6 days. It also arrives at 207–216 units against a capacity of 236, so excess stock risks being lost. So the 2-day cycle is best: candidates 0, 1, 2, 5 and 6.
2. **Order size.** A missing unit costs 11 for product 0 (margin 3 plus penalty 8) and 14 for product 1. Leftover stock carries to the next days and costs only storage. So it pays to order above forecast. Because the average multiplier is 1.046, the expected demand is about 5% above forecast.
   - Candidate 0 orders about 1.0× forecast, which is below expected demand, so it will often run short.
   - Candidate 1 orders about 1.18× forecast for product 0 and about 1.3× for product 1. The surplus builds up, gets written off when it expires (each unit lost costs 4) and incurs storage. That costs about 140 per cycle.
   - Candidate 2 orders about 1.05×, which is roughly the expected level with no safety buffer.
   - Candidates 5 and 6 order about 1.1×, a moderate buffer that grows slowly and is drained by occasional demand spikes. This is the best balance.
3. **5 against 6.** The two plans are identical up to day 22.
   - Candidate 5 places one large order on day 24 (112 and 68) to cover days 27–29, and skips day 26. That saves one 58 fee. It adds about 58 in storage over days 27–28.
   - Candidate 6's day-24 order arrives on day 27 as 78 units of product 0. That leaves only about 45 for day 28 against expected demand of about 43, so there is a real risk of running short.
   - Candidate 5 has more stock on day 28, which gives it a small edge once demand varies from the forecast.

I estimate **candidate 5** has the highest expected profit, but candidate 6 is nearly tied with it. I worked this through in my head on forecast values, without simulation.

1. **Ordering every day is too expensive (candidates 3 and 7).** About 27 orders × 58 ≈ 1566 in fees, compared with 14 × 58 ≈ 812 for plans that order every other day. Arrivals timed to each day's demand save about 500 in holding, which doesn't cover the extra ~750 in fees.

2. **Ordering every three days is also worse (candidate 4).** It saves about 230 in fees. Each delivery of about 216 units has to last three days, so extra holding costs about 500. On top of that, with leftovers the stock gets close to the 236-unit limit, and part of the delivery is lost on arrival.

3. **Among the every-other-day plans, what matters is how far orders exceed forecast.** Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. Supply is fixed in advance, so any surplus carries over as a buffer, and any deficit becomes lost sales.
   - **Candidate 0** orders about 1.0 × forecast, which is below average demand. It runs short every cycle, and each missing unit costs margin plus the 8 penalty, about 11–14.
   - **Candidate 2** orders about 1.04 × forecast, which is no margin at all: the buffer hardly grows and shortages from random swings stay common.
   - **Candidate 1** orders about 1.2 × forecast for product 0 and 1.3× for product 1. The surplus piles up: about 115 extra units of product 0 at 4 each, about 1000 more in holding, and a real risk of hitting the space limit and having units spoil.
   - **Candidates 5 and 6** order about 1.1 × forecast, about 1.14× for product 1. The buffer grows modestly and stays around 30 units of product 0 and 10 of product 1. This is the best balance between shortages and holding.

4. **Candidate 5 vs candidate 6.** They differ only at the end. Candidate 5 replaces the last two orders with one order of 112/68 on day 24. That saves one 58 fee plus about 12 in purchases. It adds about 58 in holding (about 48 for product 0 and 10 for product 1), and gives a small chance of overflow on day 27. Net, candidate 5 comes out about +12 ahead, which is within the noise. If you want the lower-risk option, candidate 6 is essentially as good.

I picked **candidate 1**. This was worked out in my head as asked, with no simulation, and candidate 6 is close behind.

1. **How often to order.** Each day with an order costs 58. Ordering every day (candidates 3 and 7) adds up to about 27 × 58 ≈ 1566 in fees, which eats most of the margin. Ordering every three days (candidate 4) brings in roughly 216 units per delivery. With leftover stock, that can go over the 236-unit capacity, and it also raises storage costs. Ordering every second day is the best trade-off, which leaves candidates 0, 1, 2, 5 and 6.
2. **Running short costs more than holding extra.**
   - Product 0: a missed sale costs 7 − 4 + 8 = 11 (lost margin plus the penalty). An extra unit costs only 0.7 a day, and it can still be sold over the following days within its 9-day shelf life.
   - Product 1: a missed sale costs 10 − 4 + 8 = 14, and an extra unit costs only 0.4 a day.
   
   So it pays to order more than the forecast. That is more true here because actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast.
3. **Comparing order sizes.**
   - Candidate 0 orders about 1.0 × forecast, so it will often run short.
   - Candidate 6 orders about 1.1 × forecast, and candidate 1 orders about 1.2 × forecast.
   - Candidate 1's extra stock builds up as a buffer. Some product 0 units will expire, costing about 4 each plus storage, but fewer shortages save about as much. For product 1 the gain clearly outweighs the cost.
   
   Candidate 1's deliveries should mostly stay under the 236-unit limit. The day 21 delivery is the one most likely to go a little over.

Candidate 1 should beat candidate 6 mainly because of the extra product 1 stock. How close the two are depends on how much expired product 0 really costs.

I chose **candidate 5**. This is an estimate worked out by reasoning, not a simulation, and the gap between 5 and 6 is small.

1. **Ordering every other day is better than ordering daily.** Candidates 3 and 7 place orders on 27 days. That costs about 1,566 in fixed fees, compared with about 812 for plans that order every two days. The difference, about 750, outweighs any gain from tracking demand more closely.

2. **Ordering every three days (candidate 4) is worse than every two.** It saves 4 order fees (about 232). But average stock rises by about half a day's demand, which adds roughly 19 per day in storage, or about 500 over the period. Its deliveries of up to 216 units also risk overflowing the 236-unit warehouse.

3. **Among the every-other-day plans, ordering above the forecast pays off.** Both products have a long shelf life relative to the order cycle, so leftover stock just carries over to the next days. Storing an extra unit costs 0.7 per day for product 0 and 0.4 for product 1. A lost sale costs 11 for product 0 (3 margin plus 8 penalty) and 14 for product 1. Also, because the plans are fixed in advance, shortfalls pile up over time like a random walk. That makes a modest built-in buffer worthwhile.
   - Candidate 0 orders exactly the forecast for product 0. That is below expected demand, since the demand multiplier averages 1.046, so it will run short often.
   - Candidate 2 orders about at expected demand, with only a small extra amount at the start.
   - Candidate 1 orders about 20% above forecast. The surplus keeps growing, raising storage costs and the risk of goods expiring or overflowing the warehouse.
   - Candidates 5 and 6 order about 10% above forecast, which is the best balance between shortage penalties and storage.

4. **Candidates 5 and 6 differ only at the end.** Candidate 5 replaces the last two orders with one order on day 24. That saves one fee (58) at the cost of about 33 in extra storage. It also orders slightly fewer units overall at the end, when leftovers are worth nothing. So candidate 5 comes out a little ahead.

I estimated this in my head without simulating it. The pick is **Candidate 6**, but its lead over Candidate 5 is small enough that either could win.

**Ordering every other day works best.**
- **Every day (Candidates 3 and 7):** about 14 more order days than the every-other-day plans. At 58 each that is roughly 800 extra in fees. The lower stock saves only about 540 in holding.
- **Every three days (Candidate 4):** saves about 4 orders, or roughly 230 in fees. The extra stock costs about 540 in holding.

**Order size.** Orders are fixed in advance, and leftovers carry over until they expire.
- **Candidate 0 (orders equal to forecast):** about 5% below expected demand, since the average multiplier is about 1.046. Each unit short costs 11–14 (lost margin plus the 8 penalty), so this loses on shortages.
- **Candidate 1 (about 1.2× forecast):** a surplus of about 10 units a day builds up and expires, at about 4 per unit plus holding.
- **Candidates 5 and 6 (about 1.1× forecast, slightly above expected demand):** this looks like the best balance.

**Candidate 6 vs 5.** They differ only at the end. Candidate 5 replaces the last two orders with one bigger order on day 24. That saves one 58 fee but adds about 62 in holding over days 27–28.

Кандидат 6, вероятно, лучший, но отрыв от 5 и 2 невелик и находится в пределах точности счёта в уме.

1. **Частота заказов.** Кандидаты 3 и 7 заказывают каждый день. Это около 27 дней × 58, то есть примерно 1566 фиксированных расходов против ~780 у планов «через день». Хранение в планах «через день» обходится дешевле этой экономии: примерно 20 ед. × 0,7 + 10 ед. × 0,4 ≈ 18 в день, или ~36 за два дня против сэкономленных 58. Кандидат 4 заказывает раз в три дня. Это экономит ещё 58 на каждые 6 дней, но добавляет ~100 хранения за тот же срок. Кроме того, поставки по 200 с лишним единиц плюс остаток рискуют не влезть в склад на 236.

2. **Объём заказов.** Недостача стоит дорого: у товара 0 это 3 упущенной маржи + 8 неустойки = 11 за единицу, у товара 1 — 6 + 8 = 14. Лишняя единица обходится всего в 0,7 или 0,4 в день, и годность 9 и 7 дней позволяет её продать позже. Средний множитель спроса 1,046, поэтому заказ ровно по прогнозу систематически отстаёт от спроса.
   - **Кандидат 0** заказывает ровно по прогнозу. Он отстаёт от спроса примерно на 4,6 % и ещё теряет на случайных колебаниях. Это сотни на неустойках.
   - **Кандидат 2** заказывает ~1,03–1,04 от прогноза и почти не держит запаса на случай колебаний. Остаток у него блуждает вокруг нуля, и недостачи будут частыми.
   - **Кандидат 1** заказывает ~1,2 от прогноза. Остаток быстро растёт, отсюда большое хранение, а в день 9 (приход 205 ед. плюс остаток) и позже склад переполняется.
   - **Кандидаты 5 и 6** заказывают ~1,1 от прогноза. Это разумный запас против колебаний при умеренном хранении.

3. **Кандидат 5 против 6.** Они отличаются только концом. Кандидат 5 экономит один заказ (58), но примерно столько же доплачивает за хранение товара под день 29 (~62). Главное: в день 27 у него приходит 112 + 68 = 180 единиц поверх накопленного остатка (~90–100). Это больше 236, и излишек товара 1 пропадает, потому что товар 0 принимается первым. Кандидат 6 в день 27 принимает 78 + 55 = 133 единицы, это около 233 с остатком, и в склад он укладывается.

I pick **candidate 6**, but with low confidence. I worked this out by hand on the forecast values rather than simulating it step by step. Candidates 5 and 6 come out almost tied.

1. **Order fees.** The daily plans (3 and 7) place about 27 orders and pay about 1,566 in fixed fees, against 812 for the every-other-day plans. That alone rules them out.
2. **Every-third-day plan (4).** Ten orders save about 232 in fees compared with ordering every other day. But it has to carry about half a day's extra demand in stock, which costs roughly 19 a day, or about 570 over 30 days. Arrivals of 144+72 also come close to the 236-unit capacity.
3. **Order size in the every-other-day plans.** The real average demand is about 1.046 × forecast.
   - **Candidate 0** orders about 1.0 × forecast, which is below average demand. That causes steady shortages: about 10 units of product 0 every two days, at 11 each (lost margin plus penalty).
   - **Candidate 2** orders about the average demand, with no spare stock building up. Shortages still cost an estimated 80 or so per cycle.
   - **Candidate 1** orders 1.2–1.3 × forecast. Extra stock piles up until it spoils: wasted purchases plus holding costs run to hundreds over the run, and arrivals start to hit the warehouse limit.
   - **Candidates 5 and 6** order about 1.10–1.15 × forecast, a moderate buffer. Running out costs much more (11–14 per unit) than holding a leftover unit (0.4–0.7 per day), so this level of excess looks like the best balance.
4. **Candidate 5 vs 6.** They differ only at the end. Candidate 5 replaces the last two orders with one order of 112+68 on day 24. That saves the 58 order fee, but day 29's goods arrive two days early, which costs about 62 in holding. The 180 units also arrive on top of the existing buffer, which risks going over the 236 limit. I chose 6 because of that overflow risk.

Я выбираю кандидата 5: у него наибольший ожидаемый итог. Всё считал в уме, грубо, поэтому уверенность умеренная, но не настолько низкая, чтобы отказаться от выбора.

**Что общее у всех.** До первого прихода на 3-й день нехватка неизбежна. Спрос на дни 0–2: товар 0 — 137 единиц при запасе 57, товар 1 — 61 при запасе 32. Этот штраф одинаков для всех планов. Денег хватает: самый крупный заказ (кандидат 1, около 700 в день 0) оплачивается со стартовых 1416, дальше поступает выручка.

**Ежедневные заказы (кандидаты 3 и 7) проигрывают.** Они платят 58 за 27 дней, то есть 1566. Планы с заказом через день платят 696–754. Лишние ~800–870 точность ежедневных заказов не окупает.

**Заказ раз в 3 дня (кандидат 4) тоже хуже.** Он экономит около 170 на сборах. Но средний оборотный запас растёт, и лишнее хранение обходится примерно в 500. К тому же приходы по 210–220 единиц плюс остаток подходят к пределу 236, и при слабом спросе часть товара пропадёт.

**Планы с заказом через день (кандидаты 0, 1, 2, 5, 6) отличаются запасом сверх прогноза.** Сравниваю с ожидаемым спросом на товар 0 в дни 3–29: 1137 по прогнозу × 1,046 ≈ 1189.
- **Кандидат 0** заказывает 1137, ровно по прогнозу, то есть ниже среднего. Он систематически недопоставляет, а нехватка товара 0 стоит около 11 за единицу (3 упущенной маржи плюс 8 неустойки).
- **Кандидат 2** заказывает около 1195, ровно по среднему, без запаса на случайность. Совокупный спрос за 27 дней колеблется примерно на ±68, так что он будет часто терять продажи.
- **Кандидат 1** заказывает 1349, то есть на ~160 больше среднего. Это около 640 на закупку лишнего плюс большое хранение растущего остатка, и к концу есть риск упереться в 236.
- **Кандидат 5** заказывает 1247: запас около 5 % сверх среднего, и по товару 1 он заказывает с бо́льшим запасом. Это разумно, потому что нехватка товара 1 стоит 14 за единицу (6 маржи плюс 8 неустойки), а хранение — всего 0,4.

**Кандидат 5 против кандидата 6.** Планы совпадают до дня 22. В конце кандидат 5 одним заказом в день 24 (112, 68) покрывает дни 27–29 и обходится без заказа в день 26. Это экономит 58, немного закупки и около 60 на хранении. Итого кандидат 5 лучше примерно на 120.

Итоговый порядок: 5 > 6 > 2 > 0 и 1 > 4 > 3 и 7.

I'd pick **candidate 5**. This comes from a rough mental check, not an exact simulation, and candidates 5, 6 and 2 are close.

1. **Ordering every day costs too much (candidates 3 and 7).** The 58 fee is charged on about 27 days, roughly 1,566 in total. Ordering every other day pays about 13 fees, roughly 754. The extra fees outweigh what better day-by-day matching saves.
2. **Ordering exactly to forecast is too little (candidate 0).** Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. Running short costs the lost margin plus the penalty, which is 11 per unit for product 0 and 14 for product 1. Unsold stock carries over to later days, so overstocking mostly costs only holding and occasional spoilage. That makes regular shortages expensive.
3. **About 20% over forecast is too much (candidate 1).** The surplus builds up with every order. Old batches start to spoil, which loses the purchase price of 4 per unit. Around day 9, the large delivery of 160 + 45 plus the leftover stock is likely to exceed the 236-unit warehouse, and anything over the limit is lost.
4. **Ordering every 3 days (candidate 4)** saves about 4 fees, around 232. But each delivery covers 3 days, so it is close to the warehouse limit (216 plus leftovers) and has more shortage risk inside each cycle.
5. **Candidates 5, 6 and 2 sit in a sensible range.** Candidates 5 and 6 order about 10% over forecast, which is about 5% over expected demand. This builds a small buffer that grows slowly and protects against shortages without much spoilage. Candidate 2 builds a buffer at the start and then orders roughly at expected demand. Its stock can then drift either way, so shortages are more likely later in the month.
6. **Candidate 5 vs 6:** they differ only at the end. Candidate 5 covers days 27–29 with one order on day 24 instead of two, which saves one 58 fee. The buffer built up by then should cover the slightly higher risk.

I picked **candidate 2** (expected profit is highest for it). This comes from rough mental estimates, not a step-by-step simulation, and its lead over candidate 6 is narrow.

**Order frequency:**
- **Daily orders (3, 7):** 27 order days cost 27 × 58 ≈ 1566 in order fees. Ordering every other day costs 13 × 58 ≈ 754. Daily ordering saves only about 570 in holding, so it doesn't pay off.
- **Every three days (4):** saves about 232 in fees (4 fewer order days). But the average stock is half a day's demand higher, which costs about 500 extra in holding. Big deliveries can also overflow the 236-unit warehouse when random demand leaves stock over.
- **Every other day (0, 1, 2, 5, 6):** this frequency wins. The candidates differ in how much they order compared with expected demand. Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.

**Why the "excess" matters.** With a fixed plan, unsold stock carries over to the next delivery and shortfalls are simply lost. So any regular surplus piles up as stock and costs holding: 0.7 a day for product 0 and 0.4 for product 1. Whatever is left at the end is wasted purchase cost.

| Candidate | Product 0 per 2 days vs expected demand | Product 1 | Main loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | about −4 (orders exactly the forecast) | about 0 | Regular shortfalls: lost margin plus penalty, ≈11 per unit |
| 1 | about +13 | about +11 | Stock builds by ~25 units per cycle: heavy holding, overflow risk, write-offs, big leftover at the end |
| 5 / 6 | about +5 | about +4 | Over 13 cycles: ≈590 holding and ≈260 leftover for product 0, against ≈250 saved on shortfalls |
| **2** | **about 0** | **about +3** | Smallest total |

**Why candidate 2:**
- It adds a buffer of 18 product 0 units (105 instead of 87) to the first order on day 0, which arrives on day 3.
- After that it orders roughly expected demand, so stock doesn't steadily grow.
- Its last orders are smaller (70 and 30), which cuts the leftover that is worthless at the end.
- It holds up best when actual demand differs from the forecast. Shortfalls stay moderate, about 40 units of product 0 over the period. Stock doesn't creep up, so it doesn't run into the warehouse limit or write-offs.

Candidate 6 comes second. It loses about 150–250 to candidate 2, mainly on holding and leftover stock.

Я выбрал кандидата 5. Это оценка в уме, без моделирования, так что результат не проверен.

- **Заказ раз в два дня лучше ежедневного.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 58, поэтому кандидаты 3 и 7, заказывающие каждый день, платят этот сбор почти вдвое чаще. Кандидат 4 заказывает раз в три дня, но крупными партиями, а это означает больше хранения и риск, что излишек пропадёт при приходе.
- **Небольшой запас сверх прогноза окупается.** Нехватка обходится дороже лишней единицы. Для товара 0 это 3 упущенной прибыли и 8 неустойки против 4 закупки плюс хранение. Для товара 1 это 6 и 8 против 4 плюс хранение. К тому же средний спрос примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза.
- **Сравнение кандидатов, заказывающих раз в два дня:**
  - Кандидат 0 заказывает ровно по прогнозу, поэтому будет чаще не хватать товара.
  - Кандидат 2 тоже близок к прогнозу, он заказывает примерно столько же, сколько кандидат 0.
  - Кандидат 1 заказывает примерно в 1,2 раза больше прогноза. Непроданный остаток не сгорает сразу и копится от цикла к циклу. От этого растёт хранение, а партии рискуют не поместиться на склад. Особенно это касается прихода в день 9, когда приходит 205 единиц сверх остатков.
  - Кандидаты 5 и 6 заказывают примерно в 1,1 раза больше прогноза, это разумная середина.
- **Кандидат 5 против кандидата 6.** Они совпадают до дня 22. В конце кандидат 5 делает один заказ в день 24 (112 и 68 единиц) вместо двух заказов в дни 24 и 26. Это экономит 58 за лишний день заказа, а закупка обходится примерно на 16 дешевле. При этом заказанного хватает на ожидаемый спрос дней 27–29: около 112 единиц товара 0 и 65 единиц товара 1.

I chose **candidate 5**. I worked this out in my head and did not run a simulation, so it's a reasoned choice rather than a computed best.

1. **Order every other day, not every day.** Each order day costs 58. Ordering daily (candidates 3 and 7) costs about 27 × 58 ≈ 1566, roughly twice what the every-other-day plans pay.
